claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening at approximately 8 dpa.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 undergoes radiation-induced precipitation at approximately 8 dpa.
The proposed intervention is addition of 0.5–2 at% yttrium.
Added yttrium will segregate to grain boundaries in the alloy.
Added yttrium will react with residual oxygen to form stable nanoscale oxide dispersoids.
Yttrium segregation and oxide dispersoids will provide defect sinks that trap irradiation-generated defects.
Trapping irradiation-generated defects will reduce the driving force for solute precipitation.
Yttrium addition will prevent radiation-induced precipitation in nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
At approximately 8 dpa, the yttrium-modified alloy will have significantly lower radiation-induced precipitate density than the unmodified alloy.
The yttrium-modified alloy will retain irradiation hardening at a similarly negligible level relative to the unmodified alloy.
Yttrium addition will improve microstructural stability.
The improved microstructural stability will enhance suitability or processability for practical bulk fabrication.
The proposed behavior applies up to approximately 8 dpa and from approximately 300 to 800°C.
Irradiation from 300 to 800°C simulates fusion-reactor service conditions.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis says yttrium will prevent precipitation, implying elimination, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification rule require only a significant but unquantified reduction in precipitate density.
